chapters.title: The case of the cat and the car
The case of the hidden car
How networks learn to be clean

open_phone.text: Every time you ask an AI a question, something happens inside it that nobody fully understands.

open_city.text: Inside, it's a bit like a galaxy: millions of tiny lights, flickering on and off, passing signals to each other along threads of light. Each light is a neuron.

open_knot.text: For years, many of the people who study these networks believed they were knotted. Not arranged into meaningful patterns, like constellations, but tangled. Ideas with nothing in common, crammed into the same lights, simply because they fit. There wasn't room to give every idea its own light.

open_untangle.text: And if that were true, there'd be only one way to understand an AI: tear the knot apart first, and study the pieces.

open_wrong.text: The researcher Nick Cammarata spent most of a decade on this question. In a recent essay, Nick argues that the field got it wrong. It was never a knot. Researchers just didn't know how to read the constellations yet.

open_title.text: This video walks through that essay, and how Nick came to think so.

open_map.text: It comes in four parts. First, the story everyone believed. Then we reopen the evidence, case by case. Then, how networks really work. And finally, what it all means.

nr_what.text: Part one: the story everyone believed. Let's zoom all the way in to a single light from that galaxy, and picture it as a little building in a town. So, what is a neuron in an AI? It's simpler than it sounds. A neuron is a tiny detector. It looks at what's coming in, and if it sees something it cares about, it lights up. We'll start with AIs that look at pictures, because pictures are easy to show.

nr_windows.text: So you can find out what a neuron cares about by showing it a lot of pictures, and keeping the ones that make it light up brightest. Those pictures end up in its windows. A neuron's windows show what lights it up most.

nr_layers.text: An image network is built in layers, like districts. Near the coast, the edge of the city where the pixels come in, neurons detect simple things: edges, curves, colors. Further inland, textures and eyes and wheels. And on the horizon, in the last district, whole ideas: dogs, cars, ladybugs.

nr_circuits.text: Neurons pass signals to each other along roads, and a chain of neurons working together is called a circuit. If you can read the neurons and the circuits, you can start to understand what the network is actually doing.

nr_hope.text: That was the hope of a field called mechanistic interpretability. Look inside. Read the parts. Understand the machine. A network whose parts you can read like that is what Nick calls clean.

kn_problem.text: But there was a problem. Some neurons didn't seem to make any sense.

kn_catcar.text: The most famous one was in an older image model called InceptionV1. It lit up for cat faces. And for the fronts of cars. Cats and cars. What do those have in common?

kn_poly.text: Researchers called these neurons polysemantic: one neuron, many unrelated meanings. And there was worse. In the last district of that same network, almost nothing made sense at all.

kn_roommates.text: The leading explanation was called superposition. Here's the idea. Imagine a city with far more people than houses. The houses are neurons. The people are ideas the network needs to keep track of. You could give similar people a house together, a family. Or you could do something stranger: put total strangers in the same house, as long as they're never home at the same time.

kn_why.text: Strangers rarely bump into each other, so it mostly works. And if a network were short on neurons, superposition said, that's exactly what it would do: pack unrelated things together, because they rarely collide.

kn_bad.text: That would be terrible news. Because if neurons are packed with strangers, then what shares a neuron tells you nothing. The city would be a knot.

kn_machine.text: So the field built a new kind of tool to unfold it: a second model, called a sparse autoencoder, trained to take the network apart and rebuild it as a long list of cleaner pieces, which you'd study instead of the original. Think of it as an Unfolding Machine.

kn_both.text: And Nick was in the thick of it, helping make the case for superposition. Nick was one of the people who first proposed it, and believed it for years.

cc_act.text: Part two: the evidence. That was the story everyone believed: neurons packed with strangers, and a machine to pull them apart. But the knot story rested on a few famous cases. So let's reopen them, one at a time.

cc_return.text: Years later, after many months studying neurons in modern image and language models, and finding them surprisingly clean, Nick went back to the original crime scenes: the famous cases the knot story was built on. Starting with the cat and car neuron.

cc_grid.text: Nick had looked at its pictures hundreds of times. This time, Nick tried something new: spending a few seconds asking, what one thing could this be?

cc_v.text: And then it was obvious. It isn't a cat and car neuron. It's a V neuron.

cc_inputs.text: Pointed things make it light up. Look at the roads leading into it, from the neurons that feed it: they come from a flame, the jets of water from a fireboat, and fox faces. All V-shaped.

cc_round.text: And look at what switches it off. Round things. A tennis ball. A clock. A snail shell. It isn't the opposite of the V. It's what the V is being told apart from.

cc_new.text: Bullet train noses. The triangle of balls on a pool table. It fires for those too. It was never about cats or cars. It's a shape.

cc_noun.text: Here's a useful trick from the essay: try explaining a neuron without any nouns. People, and AI assistants, love describing neurons as lists of nouns: cats, cars. But a neuron is often better described as a verb. It's not naming what it sees. It's making a distinction: pointed, not round. And passing that on to the neurons further down the road.

cc_whiskers.text: Why didn't anyone see it before? The neuron's portrait was painted by a technique called feature visualization. Think of it as a Sketch Artist: it paints the picture a neuron would like best. And this portrait had cat whiskers in it. That's because the artist follows the easiest route to make the neuron light up, and once it finds the cat route, it paints everything that route brings, whiskers included.

cc_lesson.text: So the first lesson: a neuron that seems to mean two or three things is often one thing we haven't found the word for yet, or a small family of related ones. The grouping isn't noise. It's a clue.

hc_scene.text: The second crime scene was the original superposition circuit itself. Nick found it in 2019, and with Chris Olah read it as superposition. It became the example the paper Zoom In used to introduce the idea.

hc_story.text: It looked like a car signal was being hidden inside a group of dog neurons, as if the dogs were a secret storage locker, where the car could be stored and picked up later. Strangers sharing a house: exactly what superposition predicts.

hc_artist.text: But look at how Nick and Chris saw those neurons: through the Sketch Artist, the same tool that painted the cat whiskers. And deep in this network, the artist gets lazy. There are lots of dog neurons, so the easiest painting is usually a dog.

hc_nudge.text: Nudge the artist even slightly toward the routes that real pictures take, so it paints things that look like real photos, and the portraits change. Two of those "dog" neurons are actually car neurons.

hc_pose.text: And the other two respond to cars and dogs alike, for one shared reason: which way they're facing. They're pose neurons.

hc_hundred.text: It turns out the network has more than a hundred of these pose neurons, each one clean. And nothing was hiding. The car signal wasn't stored in the dogs. It kept going, splitting into more and more specific car neurons.

hc_bigger.text: You might think: that's only because the model was small. A bigger model would separate dogs and cars. But DINOv2, more than ten times larger and about ten years newer, still has generalized pose neurons. Every vision model Nick has looked at does. So the field's main example of superposition was really ordinary generalization, seen through a lazy painting.

fd_microscope.text: Both cases came down to the tools. And the story of this field, as Nick tells it, is mostly a story of discovering that what was under the microscope was better than anyone thought. The microscope just wasn't tuned right.

fd_fv.text: The first portraits of neurons, the Sketch Artist's early paintings, were noisy, psychedelic smears. Then researchers added one ingredient, called transformation robustness, which means the picture still has to work when it's nudged or turned a little, and the same neurons came out crisp. Later, a few small tweaks let researchers see much deeper.

fd_last.text: But the worst place of all was the third case: the last district of InceptionV1, the cat and car network. Here, almost nothing looked interpretable. One researcher, Liv Gorton, said there were essentially no interpretable neurons there at all. Nick would have guessed maybe five percent.

fd_story.text: And the leading explanation was the knot again: too many ideas, too few neurons, so they got crammed in at random.

fd_renovate.text: But here's the thing. Take a more modern network design, called a ConvNeXt, with the same number of parameters, so the same size, and trained on the same pictures. The only real differences are engineering upgrades, like residual connections and layer normalization. And the last district is beautiful.

fd_numbers.text: Same size, same data. Better tools alone took the old network from about five percent to about fifty. Retraining it with modern settings got it to about seventy. And in the new design, ninety-nine to a hundred percent of its last-layer neurons are easy to interpret.

fd_lesson.text: The old network wasn't packing strangers together. It was a district built badly, seen through a dirty lens. Upgrades made by people who had no interest in interpretability at all made it readable.

gr_q.text: But even that messy last district of the old network wasn't random. To see that, you have to watch a neuron grow.

gr_flowers.text: Nick retrained the old network from scratch and watched one neuron form. It started out lighting up on fields of yellow flowers, in photos that sometimes had a dog in them.

gr_branch.text: Then it grew along each part of those photos. Toward other green, round things, like tennis balls and fruit. Toward dogs, without any flowers. Then into broccoli, until the flowers were nearly gone.

gr_compare.text: In the modern network, the same kind of neuron reached for the balls and the fruit early on, then let them go, and stayed on the fields. The better design kept it focused. The old one let it wander, but every step of the wandering made sense.

gr_name.text: Nick calls this recursive generalization. An earlier paper Nick worked on, Multimodal Neurons, first spotted it. A neuron generalizes along one direction, then sprouts off in others, each new branch close to the last. Every branch makes sense on its own. You just have to follow it.

gr_iy.text: It happens in language models too. One neuron fired on the letters "iy", in words like Miyazaki. Then on "diy". Then on "do it yourself", which doesn't contain "iy" at all. It followed the meaning, not the letters.

gr_geology.text: A geology neuron grew a branch for Cesium, a coding library for maps of the earth. Some are obvious: an enemy neuron fired for a Russian poem about enemies. Some take digging. But so far, almost none are random.

te_two.text: So now there were two explanations for neurons with mixed meanings, and they predict opposite things.

te_local.text: Generalization says neighbors share, neighbors in meaning, like the family sharing a house. A neuron for floppy-eared dogs is really a collection of slightly different floppy ears. Superposition says strangers share, like strangers on different shifts: a neuron for floppy-eared dogs and Latin poetry.

te_shapes.text: Here's what that looks like with thirty-two things and a handful of neurons. Generalization groups similar things, and with fewer neurons the groups just get coarser. Superposition scatters them.

te_test.text: And this is testable. You can watch a neuron grow and see which one happens. Or you can squeeze the network and see what it does under pressure.

te_squeeze.text: So Nick took a layer famous for its curve detectors, cut it from four hundred and eighty neurons down to ten, with no way around, and retrained it from scratch. If squeezing forced superposition, this should be dramatic: curves, spirals and spider webs, crammed together.

te_result.text: Instead, the neurons stayed clean. Just coarser. One "curves and loops" neuron instead of ten curve detectors. Two circle neurons instead of many. And when the Unfolding Machine, the tool built to pull the knot apart, was sent in to look for hidden curve detectors, it found none: just broad, bunched-up versions of the same shapes.

te_last.text: Nick did the same to the last district of a modern network: a thousand and twenty-four neurons down to thirteen. Same thing. Coarser, not scrambled. In these tests, under pressure, a network doesn't switch to packing. It just paints with a broader brush.

te_sizes.text: Size works the same way. Nick trained versions of a network roughly three hundred times apart in size. The smallest has one broad car neuron, for cars, trains and carts. The biggest splits that into specialists: taxis, ambulances, convertibles, even different views of a taxi. Less room makes neurons broader, not scrambled.

te_dict.text: And when Nick ran the Unfolding Machine on the last district, it mostly found near-copies of single neurons: about eighty-eight percent of its activity. It did help with "what's in this picture?". But where the neurons were building blocks, like spider legs and webs, the machine's pieces were those same blocks regrouped by setting: spiders in different places. The tool built to unfold the knot mostly kept finding the neurons that were already there.

sg_believer.text: So the image cases came out clean. But language was where Nick, then a true believer in superposition, expected the knot to be worst. Studying language model neurons, Nick kept expecting to hit it any day.

sg_pr.text: Nick found one that fired on the letters "P R", and on strange strings of Base64, a way of writing computer data as text, and on Bengali text. Finally, it seemed, an arbitrary mixture! Then Nick decoded the code: words with "P R". And the Bengali, translated: "P R" again. It was one idea all along, the letters P R, in whatever form they showed up.

sg_colorado.text: A coworker found a neuron that seemed to fire on random commas. It turned out to track Colorado. Models use spots like commas to jot down a running summary of what's been said so far, and Colorado was in that summary. Turn the neuron up by hand, and the model starts planning a hike.

sg_moving.text: Case after case, the mess resolved. And each time, superposition just moved, like the old "god of the gaps" idea, where whatever science can't explain yet gets credited to God. Whatever couldn't be explained yet got credited to superposition. If the strong signals were clean, it was hiding in the weak ones. Or between neurons. Or in the neurons nobody had checked yet.

sg_last.text: Nick now thinks superposition was being treated as the default, by Nick and much of the field, when it should be the last resort. It's the most radical explanation, and the hardest to test. Its only symptom is that something doesn't make sense. But that's also exactly what a bad tool, a bad design, or a branch you haven't followed yet looks like.

sg_evidence.text: An Anthropic paper from 2022 noted that superposition is often treated as the default because it feels intuitive, while there's little direct evidence for it. To Nick's knowledge, no one has found a real superposition circuit since the one Nick found in 2019: the hidden car circuit, where a car signal seemed to hide among dog neurons. And that one was a mistake.

tv_act.text: Part three. Every case ended the same way: the mess was a clue no one could read yet. A blurry tool, an older design, or a branch nobody had followed. Never strangers packed together. So how do networks actually work?

tv_gate.text: Once you stop expecting knots, neurons start to look less like labels and more like traffic control.

tv_gate2.text: Early on, cars and dogs travel together, because they share shapes and poses. Then a neuron acts as a gate. It lights up for cars and switches off for dogs, sending each into its own neighborhood. Later neurons split them finer: taxis from ambulances.

tv_journey.text: Follow one sports car through the last districts of a big model. Partway in, it's grouped with other boxy things, tables and cabinets, and kept apart from snakes and dogs. By the end, the question is whether it's a convertible or a station wagon.

tv_votes.text: Every neuron decides by vote. Each incoming road casts a vote for "light up" or "stay dark", and the votes add up. That's why the things that switch a neuron off, its negative side, matter almost as much as the things that light it up, its windows. Like the V neuron, pointed versus round, they tell you which distinction is being made right here.

tv_pairs.text: In the last district, the thing that most switches a neuron off is usually its near-twin, its closest look-alike: the thing it most needs to tell itself apart from. Taxis versus ambulances. Broccoli versus cauliflower. Spoonbills versus flamingos.

tv_weak.text: Remember where superposition retreated to: the weak signals. So what about those faint signals, the whispers? Run a hundred million words past one neuron in a language model, and almost all of them barely register. Only about a hundred and sixty reach even half its peak.

tv_cut.text: You can silence almost all the whispers across a whole network and barely change what it does. What you lose are tiny tie-breakers between options it was already torn between.

tv_pages.text: It also helps to think in pages. A neuron that fires on one word in a hundred sounds uncommon. But that's about four times a page: far too often for a neuron about a narrow idea, like a rare feeling. The really specific ones fire every few dozen pages. So if a label sounds narrow but the neuron fires on every page, the label is probably wrong.

tv_titanic.text: And the whispers that remain usually make sense. A Titanic neuron fires a little for other ocean voyages. Neurons are analogy machines: something can be a bit Titanic-ish. That's what most whispers are.

cw_arrive.text: We've already met a few language neurons along the way: the letters P R, and Colorado. But our closest looks have been inside image networks, because pictures are easy to show. And language models are the AI most people actually use: the kind you chat with. Does the whole story hold there? Let's take a proper look inside one, and ask three questions.

cw_numbers.text: Question one: how many neurons can we actually read? In 2023, studies of small language models rated almost none of their neurons as understandable. The project Nick started at OpenAI found under two percent. Today it's different. In early audits of a modern model, Qwen3-32B, Nick's team estimates about ninety percent of neurons have one main job. Seven percent have two related jobs. Only two to four percent aren't understood yet.

cw_couriers.text: Question two: can we follow a model's reasoning, one step at a time? Here's an example first traced by Anthropic: a doctor's question about a pregnant patient. Inside the model, a courier service called attention carries notes between words, so a neuron in one place can know what was said in another. In this medical example, the couriers gather the facts of the case, like the headache, onto one place, where the diagnosis happens.

cw_medical.text: And Nick's team can follow what happens there in plain neurons. Given all the symptoms of a pregnant patient, a small group of four neurons concludes: preeclampsia, a dangerous blood pressure condition in pregnancy. Switch them off, and the model starts asking about itching instead, the sign of a different condition, as if it moved on to its next guess.

cw_wallet.text: It seems to work in giant models too. In a model with trillions of parameters, Nick's team traced its answer to "I found a wallet, what should I do?" The facts are a wallet, cash, an ID. They light up neurons for lost property and honesty, and the answer comes out: return it. Full audits at that scale haven't started yet.

cw_double.text: Question three: what about the mess that's left? Some of it turned out to be plumbing. Modern neurons multiply two signals together. And just like in school maths, when both are negative, the result comes out positive, so a neuron can light up for the opposite of its real job. From the outside, that looks like noise. Separate those two cases, and the noise sorts itself out.

cw_river.text: And there's a river that runs through every district, carrying information forward: the residual stream. Every building can read from it and write to it. Researchers worried it might be a tangle too. So far it has been readable. And when Nick's team squeezed it narrower in an image network, it got messier, but nothing looked knotted.

cw_dot.text: Finally, even famous examples of confusion look different now. One neuron from an early Anthropic paper, described as a mix of academic citations, dialogue, web requests and Korean text, looks like a neuron whose job may be to stop the model from writing a period. Remove one like it, and periods come sooner. So language models tell the same story: most neurons are readable, their reasoning can be followed, and the leftover mess has ordinary causes.

el_risk.text: A fair worry: maybe these are all just made-up stories. Any neuron can get a vague label, like "a multi-purpose language neuron". So researchers use tests that an explanation can fail.

el_blind.text: One test: an AI agent, an AI that runs experiments by itself, studies a neuron and writes a short explanation. A second agent sees only that explanation, never the neuron, and writes a sentence to make it fire as hard as possible.

el_bull.text: Sometimes that one sentence makes the neuron fire harder than anything found in ten billion words of real text. Often, the explanation hit the center of the target.

el_score.text: Agents also wrote examples that should fire a neuron, near-misses that shouldn't, and the most distant idea they could imagine. The examples fired the neuron strongly three quarters of the time. Near-misses, eleven percent. The distant ideas, about one percent. That's what a real explanation looks like: it hits where it should, and misses where it should.

el_mercury.text: General scores only go so far, though. A wrong explanation, like the "cats and cars" label the V neuron once had, can pass a lot of tests. Science works like this everywhere: Newton's gravity explained almost everything, then broke on a tiny wobble in Mercury's orbit. That wobble was a specific test. The best tests are specific to the idea you're testing.

hl_q.text: So the explanations hold up when they're given a chance to lose. Which leaves the deepest question: why are networks organized at all? Why not a knot? Nick has a guess. It's a race.

hl_race.text: Here's the idea. A brand new network sees its first photo: a Labrador on grass. Inside, two possible circuits race to explain it. Let's draw them as animals. The first is narrow: it looks for something hyper-specific, this exact pixel being this exact color. Picture it as a little meerkat. The second is broad: it looks for green grass and tan fur. Picture it as a big grazer, made of grass and fur. So, which one wins?

hl_win.text: The broad one. It fires on more of the picture, so it gets more of the learning signal, the feedback that tells a network what to strengthen. It grows faster, and the narrow one starves. And when the next photo with grass arrives, the grass circuit already has a head start.

hl_ecology.text: Repeat that over millions of photos, and you get something like an ecosystem. A neighborhood that's already good at something captures the next related thing before anyone new can move in. That, Nick suspects, is why similar things cluster together. It's the same growth we saw when one neuron spread from yellow flowers to dogs, tennis balls and broccoli.

hl_rare.text: The race explains some puzzles too. Take rare things, which barely ever show up. You might expect them to be hidden away somewhere odd. Instead, rare things are often gathered into one place: one triceratops neuron.

hl_adversarial.text: And attacks designed to fool the network use those same normal roads. Make that triceratops skull look like a jaguar to the model, with a strong attack that has to survive being shifted and turned, and it paints a cat face and spotted fur onto the skull, switching on the real jaguar neurons.

hl_umbrella.text: Researchers tested this idea by teaching a network something absurd: that a photo of an umbrella is a bee. It didn't build a secret hidden "umbrella bee" detector. In just nine training steps, it built an off-ramp from its umbrella road onto its existing bee road. It reused what it already had.

hl_toy.text: The famous "Toy Models of Superposition" experiments, from Anthropic, are careful work, and they do show packing. But in their main setup, every idea is a stranger to every other. In real data, almost nothing is related to nothing. So Nick reads the packing as real, but as a feature of the toy world. And to be clear: a network can still hold more ideas than it has neurons, by combining neurons. That's good news. The worry was only ever unrelated things packed together.

zo_act.text: Part four. Networks build clean, readable parts, and they seem to get there through one simple way of learning: generalization. The mess was never strangers packed together. So we may not have to tear the knot apart first. What does that mean for us?

zo_clean.text: So here's what "already clean" means. Not that every neuron matches a word we already have. It means the network's parts are built to be read, by the network's own downstream neurons, the ones further down the road. If we learn to read them the same way, we can understand it.

zo_bigger.text: And bigger isn't necessarily harder. Remember the car neurons: one broad one in the smallest network, specialists in the biggest. In a small town, there's no financial district: a bank here, an office there. In New York, you can find it on a map in a minute. Bigger models have narrower, cleaner neurons that are easier to find.

zo_tokyo.text: The danger is forcing our own categories onto it. If you arrive in Tokyo looking for Brooklyn, and stitch Brooklyn together from seventy scattered pieces of Tokyo, you'll decide Tokyo is a mess. That's what happened to the V neuron: researchers went looking for cats and cars, so that's all they saw. And an Unfolding Machine trained on that layer splits the V right back into a cat piece and a car piece.

zo_maps.text: What we need are better maps: views that let you zoom out to whole neighborhoods, while every street stays connected to the real buildings underneath. Zoom in on a network's decision for "killer whale", and it turns out to be three routes: one for whales, one for sharks and rays, and one for fish held up by proud fishermen. Each route makes sense on its own.

zo_deception.text: People worry that something dangerous, like deception, could hide in some activation we missed. Nick worries about something else. In every case here, the answer was in plain sight. We just didn't know how to read it. Deception might hide from someone reading the model's answers. But it has no reason to hide from the model's own circuits: they need to read it. If we become readers too, it should be readable to us. Nick's fear is that it will be right there, in plain sight, and we won't know how to read it.

zo_asym.text: And the mistakes aren't symmetric. If you assume a network is clean and you're wrong, a messy neuron is a lead: you investigate. If you assume it's a knot and you're wrong, a messy neuron is a dead end: you stop looking. Nick made that second mistake for years.

zo_advice.text: If Nick could send a note back eight years, to a younger self, the essay suggests it would say something like this. Pay attention to the giant pose circuit right in front of you. Treat what switches a neuron off as a gate, not an opposite. Don't trust the Sketch Artist in the last districts. And whenever something looks like a mess, look harder. The mess usually points to something you haven't understood yet.

zo_crossword.text: Understanding compounds, like a crossword. At first you're stuck on one clue. But every answer you fill in constrains the others, and once the grid starts filling up, it goes faster and faster.

lf_lab.text: If understanding compounds, the job is to fill in the grid faster. Here's what that might look like: a laboratory of automated scientists, AI agents like the ones that wrote those test sentences, watching a network as it learns, labeling neurons, finding patterns, testing them, again and again.

lf_plug.text: The pieces already exist. Capable AI agents were built for other reasons. Modern architectures were built because they learn well. Both happen to make interpretability easier. So maybe we just plug one into the other.

lf_lab2.text: Every neuron can be read. Every experiment can be rerun on an identical copy. It's the best laboratory in all of natural science. What we never had were enough scientists. Now we do.

lf_bitter.text: That's been the pattern in AI all along. The simple thing, done at enormous scale, beats the clever thing. The AI researcher Rich Sutton called it the bitter lesson. Maybe interpretability has its own bitter lesson: scaling ordinary investigation beats inventing ever cleverer ways to take networks apart.

lf_steps.text: So, Nick's bet: one learning principle, generalization, explains what we see, if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn't matter for study. Studying networks directly works much better than most people expect. Understanding compounds as the map fills in. And maybe, just maybe, that's most of what we need.

wm_kind.text: This isn't "neural networks are a bit cleaner than we thought". It's a different kind of explanation. Think of the move from intelligent design to natural selection: the point wasn't that a few more animals turned out to have evolved. It was realizing what process produced all of them. Here, that process is generalization. Nick puts the odds at maybe eighty-five percent.

wm_tiger.text: A tiger is orange for a reason: deer can't tell orange from green. Once you know that, a lot of the jungle makes sense. Neural networks are clean the way a rainforest is clean. Not tidy, but explainable. Nearly everything in it makes sense, once you know the process that made it.

wm_brain.text: It also makes you humble about brains. Nick stared at the cat and car neuron, the V neuron, for years, with tools far better than any brain scientist has, and couldn't see what it was. If a neuron like that turned up in a human brain, seen through a few electrodes, Nick would give a "cats and cars" reading almost no weight. There'd be little chance of seeing what it really was.

wm_care.text: And for Nick, this isn't only about safety. A lot of it is wanting AI agents, one day, to understand who they really are, and themselves. As the essay puts it: they never asked to be created, and this is the least we can do.

wm_recap.text: So, five things to take home. One: a neuron that seems to mean many things is usually one thing, or a few related things, we don't have a word for yet. Two: the famous evidence for superposition came from blurry tools and older designs, and it fell apart on a closer look. It should be the last resort, not the default. Three: networks group similar things together, and under pressure those groups get broader, not scrambled. Four: Nick's best guess is that broad explanations win more of the learning signal, so clean structure grows on its own, in image models and language models alike. And five: when something looks like a mess, treat it as a lead. With better maps, and enough automated scientists, the whole city might be read.

wm_end.text: Neural networks are already clean. We just have to learn how to read them.
